sections.h2: Anderson city taxes and the county offices
sections.html: The city of Anderson is the county seat, tucked into South Carolina's northwest corner roughly halfway along I-85. At the 2020 Census it had 28,106 residents, while the county surrounding it had 203,718. Sellers should know that the two are separate layers of government with one shared cashier: the city's tax bill is collected by county staff, so your calls go to the county Treasurer.

sections.h2: Bills, due date and penalty steps
sections.html:
Count on October 1 for the bill to arrive and January 15 as the last day to pay without penalty. Payment is made at the Anderson County Annex, 401 East River Street, and the Treasurer's line is (864) 260-4033.

After January 15 the city assesses a 15 percent penalty, built from three state-law steps that kick in on January 16, February 2 and March 17: 3 percent, then 7 percent more, then 5 percent more. Once March 17 is behind you, the treasurer may issue a tax execution covering taxes, penalties and costs.

Payment options include a visit to the Anderson or Powdersville office, a check in the mail, or an online payment that adds a convenience fee when you use a card. A lender that pays from escrow needs your notice forwarded to it.

A legal residence is taxed at a 4 percent assessment ratio, and most other real property at 6 percent. The lower ratio does not happen on its own. The owner applies to the assessor right after moving in, with a cutoff of January 15, the same day taxes are due. Second homes, vacation homes and rentals are left out.

Disagree with your value? The route has four stops:

  • Within 90 days of the assessment notice, send the assessor a written objection that includes your market value estimate and documents.
  • When the assessor answers, you have 30 days to appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals.
  • When the board rules, 30 more days are available to ask the Administrative Law Court for a contested case hearing.
  • If the matter is still open on December 31, a written request can get you a bill at 80 percent of the protested value.

None of this pauses the due date or excuses a late penalty. The county takes one form per parcel and returns forms that are unsigned or lack support.

sections.h2: How a sale changes the value
sections.html:
Nearly every sale counts as an assessable transfer of interest. The new owner's value is reset to full fair market value in the year after the transfer, without the 15 percent cap that protects long-time owners. Deeds, trust conveyances and distributions under a will count as transfers, though some family transfers and foreclosures before the redemption period ends are excepted.

The buyer has to file for the 4 percent rate on a house they will live in. If the property stays at 6 percent, a 25 percent ATI exemption form is available and is due January 30 of the following year.

As the seller, you are mostly spared. Your bill for the year of sale rides on the value already on the roll, and the reset shows up in what the buyer pays next year.

Ignored taxes can end in a delinquent tax sale. After one, the owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor has twelve months to redeem by paying the taxes, penalties and costs, plus interest on the bid amount that rises by quarter from 3 percent to 12 percent.

Selling first is usually cleaner. The closing agent pays the back taxes out of your proceeds. And if the title changed during the year and the new owner never got a notice, state law directs the treasurer to waive the penalties.

  • Request a payoff figure that is good through your closing date.
  • Ask the closing attorney how this year's bill will be divided.
  • If the land was farmed, check for rollback tax. Buyer and seller agree at closing on who pays it.

sections.h2: Cash sale when tax is due
sections.html:
With a cash buyer the tax is paid from the sale price at closing, so nothing comes out of your pocket at the table. Give the closing attorney your most recent bill and any past-due notices, and the attorney asks the county Treasurer for the payoff.

Cash Home Buyers purchases houses in Anderson in their current condition, including ones with deferred repairs, tenants or inherited title. Tell us about the property, what is owed and your timing, and we will say plainly whether we can make an offer.

Before you talk to any buyer, collect the latest bill, any past-due notice, the deed or estate papers, and a note of where tax mail has been going. An early handoff to the closing attorney matters, because the payoff letter takes time and its good-through date must reach your closing day.

faqs.q: When are Anderson, SC property taxes due?
faqs.a: By January 15. Bills are mailed October 1, and the 15 percent penalty is applied after January 15.

faqs.q: Where do I pay City of Anderson property tax?
faqs.a: At the Anderson County Annex, 401 East River Street, or at the Powdersville office, by mail or online. The phone is (864) 260-4033.

faqs.q: Do I get the 4 percent rate automatically after buying in Anderson?
faqs.a: No. The buyer files a legal residence application with the county assessor after moving in, and the deadline is January 15.

faqs.q: How long do I have to dispute an Anderson assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days from the assessment notice, in writing. With no notice, an appeal received before January 15 counts toward that tax year.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Anderson house that has delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing agent pays the back taxes, penalties and costs from your proceeds, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff that matches your closing date.
